h1: SEO for nonprofits chasing donors, grants and volunteers at once
metaTitle: SEO for Nonprofits: Donors, Grants, Volunteers
metaDescription: SEO for nonprofits in India. We rank cause, impact and 80G tax benefit content that brings retail donors, CSR partners and volunteers to the right pages.
answer: A nonprofit website has to serve three strangers at once: a retail donor checking whether the 80G receipt is real, a CSR manager checking your CSR-1 and FCRA status before a grant, and a volunteer looking for the nearest project. Those are three different searches, and they need three different landing pages.
takeaways: Most NGO sites are built for one audience — the retail donor — and leave the two that fund everything to guess.
Publish registration numbers as text, not badges. 12A, 80G, CSR-1, FCRA, Darpan ID. A CSR manager runs a compliance filter before reading your mission.
Since the new tax regime became the default, an 80G-led donation pitch is arguing to a shrinking audience. Lead with what the money does.
Your annual report is a PDF, which is where good content goes to be ignored. Publish it as pages.
`Where to donate clothes in Pune` is real, repeated demand that almost no Indian NGO answers.

sections.h2: Three visitors, three completely different searches
body: A nonprofit is the only kind of organisation we work with that has to sell three different things on one domain — money from individuals, money from companies, and time from strangers. Each buyer arrives on a different query and needs a different kind of proof. Most Indian NGO sites answer only the first, and answer it with a photograph and a Donate button.

table.caption: One website, three audiences, three sets of proof.
head: Who's searching
Roughly what they type
What has to be on the page they land on
rows: `donate for girl child education india`, `80g donation ngo`, `best ngo to donate to in india`
Registration numbers, where the money goes, the receipt process explained before they give, and a donation form that works one-handed on a phone
`csr partner ngo education`, `csr-1 registered ngo maharashtra`, `ngo for csr funding`
CSR-1 number, audited accounts, FCRA status, districts you actually operate in, evaluation method, and a named person with a direct email
`volunteer opportunities in bengaluru`, `ngo near me to volunteer`, `weekend teaching volunteer`
The nearest project, the real time commitment, what happens after they apply, and a form under six fields
`where to donate clothes in pune`, `donate old books ngo`, `donate wheelchair near me`
What you accept and what you don't, collection address and timings, whether you pick up and within what radius
Annual reports as web pages, financials, board and leadership, a press page and someone to contact

bullets: **In-kind donation queries are the biggest unserved demand in Indian nonprofit search.** They're answered almost entirely by blogs and city listicles rather than by the organisations that would happily collect the goods.
**Don't merge them onto one Donate page.** Three audiences, three landing pages, three calls to action. A CSR manager who lands on a retail donation form leaves.

sections.h2: The trust block, and the tax rule that changed the pitch
body: Nobody gives money to a stranger on the internet without checking something first. In India the checks are unusually specific, which is good news — it means the reassurance is a list of numbers rather than an exercise in adjectives.
Put them in text, in the footer and on the donation and CSR pages. Text, not an image of a certificate, because a number in an image can't be copied into a government portal.
bullets: **12A / 12AB registration and 80G approval**, with numbers and validity dates.

**Your receipt process, described.** You file the annual statement of donations and the donor gets their certificate for the claim. A donor who has claimed 80G before knows exactly what that means, and saying it plainly beats any seal.
**FCRA registration number**, if you're eligible to receive foreign contributions, along with the fact that those funds are received only into the designated FCRA account as the law requires.
**NGO Darpan unique ID** from NITI Aayog, and your **CSR-1 registration number** — the one a corporate donor's compliance team will ask for first.
**Audited financials and the last three annual reports**, with the auditor named and the year stated.
**Named leadership and board with real bios.** For a sector judged almost entirely on trust, this is what [E-E-A-T](/glossary/e-e-a-t) actually looks like in practice.

callout.title: The 80G argument speaks to fewer people every year
callout.body: The new income tax regime is now the default, and taxpayers who stay in it can't claim an 80G deduction at all. Publishing your 80G status still matters — it's a legitimacy signal as much as a tax one, and it matters a great deal to donors on the old regime. But a donation page whose main argument is the tax break is arguing to a shrinking audience. Lead with what the money does.

sections.h2: CSR pages written for a manager with a compliance checklist
body: Companies past a size threshold have to spend a share of their profits on CSR under the Companies Act, and since the 2021 rules the implementing agency must be registered with the ministry — that's the CSR-1 number. Which means a corporate manager shortlisting partners is running a compliance filter before they get anywhere near your mission statement.
Almost no Indian NGO has a page written for that person. They have a "Partner with us" link that opens a contact form, and they wonder why corporate money arrives only through personal networks.
bullets: **A dedicated CSR partnership page**, titled the way it's searched: CSR partner, the cause, the state. Not a paragraph on the donations page.
**Compliance facts at the top**: CSR-1, 12A, 80G, FCRA where relevant, Darpan ID, years operating, audited accounts, last three annual reports.
**Programmes described as fundable units**, with a cost per unit and arithmetic you can defend if someone asks how you got there.

**Precise geography — district and block, not "across India".** CSR budgets are frequently directed to the areas where the company operates, so naming your actual districts is a matching signal for exactly the searches you want.
**A named person, a direct email and a phone number.** A generic info@ address loses more corporate conversations than a weak programme does.
**Your evaluation approach**: baseline, method, who verifies, how often. This is the difference between a partner and a recipient.

sections.h2: Your annual report is a PDF, which is where content goes to be ignored
body: Every nonprofit produces the most credible content in its sector once a year and then buries it in a four-megabyte download. PDFs can be indexed, but they can't be internally linked properly, can't carry a call to action, can't be updated in place, and are genuinely painful on a phone — which is where most of your donors are.
Publish the substance as web pages and keep the PDF as a download for the people who want the designed version.
numbered: **One permanent page per programme**, updated each year, rather than a fresh post every year competing with the last one for the same query.
**Every headline number gets a method note** — who counted, over what period, against what baseline. A number without one is a number a CSR manager will quietly discount.
**Stories with consent.** Beneficiary names and photographs need permission, and children need a stricter standard than most nonprofit websites currently apply. Anonymised is better than unconsented.
**Link the PDF from the page**, don't replace the page with it.
**Date everything and say when it was last verified.** An impact page with no date is an impact page nobody will cite.

sections.h2: Volunteers and in-kind donations are local search
body: Volunteer and in-kind demand behaves like any other local service query. Someone types a city, Google shows a map, and the organisations with a properly built profile and a city page get the applications. The rest get an email six months later from someone who found them through a friend.
bullets: **A [Google Business Profile](/glossary/google-business-profile) for every centre you genuinely staff**, with correct hours, photos and a category that matches what happens there.
**One page per city where you run something**, naming the project, the address, what happens there and who to contact. Not a single Locations page listing fourteen cities in a table.

**State the real commitment on volunteer pages**: hours per week, minimum duration, weekday or weekend, remote or on-site, training involved, police verification if you work with children. Vagueness produces applications that never turn up.
**A collection page per city for in-kind donations** — what you accept, what you can't use, timings, and whether you collect and within what radius. This is the demand nobody is answering.
**Keep the form short.** Six fields. Every extra field on a volunteer form costs you people who were willing an hour ago.

sections.h2: Google Ad Grants alongside organic, and the rules that switch it off
body: Eligible nonprofits can receive up to $10,000 a month of in-kind Google Search advertising through Ad Grants. It is comfortably the best-value channel available to an Indian NGO, and it's also the one most likely to be quietly suspended because nobody read the policy. Eligibility runs through Google's validation partner, so have your registration documents ready before you start.

It doesn't replace organic. It buys the head terms you'll spend two years earning, while your pages compound underneath — and it keeps working when the account is between rebuilds. If you're weighing the two against each other, the trade-offs are in [SEO versus paid search](/compare/ppc-vs-seo).
bullets: **Search only, and capped at a $2 maximum cost per click** unless you move to conversion-based smart bidding. It won't win expensive commercial auctions and isn't meant to.
**The account must hold a 5% click-through rate.** That single rule kills most grant accounts, because they were built on broad keywords that attract everybody and interest nobody.
**No single-word keywords and no overly generic ones.** Conversion tracking has to be live and has to track something that matters — a donation, an application, an enquiry.
**Structural requirements**: at least two ad groups per campaign, two ads per group, sitelinks, and geo-targeting that reflects where you work.
**Point it at the right pages.** A grant campaign sending volunteer searches to a donation form is the most common reason the click-through rate collapses.

callout.title: If you can't justify a retainer, don't hire one
callout.body: We charge from ₹75,000 a month and for a lot of Indian nonprofits that money is better spent on the programme. If that's you: get the Ad Grant running, publish the trust block, turn three annual reports into web pages, and build a city page for each project. That's most of the available value and it costs staff time rather than fees. Come back when the funding base can carry it.

sections.h2: What this costs, and what we actually guarantee
body: Our SEO runs from ₹75,000 a month, with smaller sites from ₹40,000, ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter and every asset stays yours. Full numbers are on [pricing](/pricing), and the general shape of budgets at this scale is in [SEO cost for a small business](/cost/seo-cost-for-small-business).

One honest complication specific to this sector: Indian giving spikes before 31 March, because of the financial year, and again around Diwali. A trailing-90-day baseline frozen in March is a much harder bar than one frozen in July. We set it from whichever quarter you actually start in and note the seasonality in writing rather than quietly picking a flattering window — the guarantee is worth nothing if the baseline was chosen to be beaten.

That baseline is your own trailing-90-day count of qualified actions from organic search — donations, CSR enquiries or volunteer applications, whichever you nominate as the one that matters. Miss it in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it. We never promise a specific ranking position, because nobody controls Google's index.

faqs.q: Do nonprofits actually need SEO, or is social media enough?
faqs.a: Social reaches people who already follow you. Search reaches the person deciding right now where to give, which company to partner with, or where to volunteer this Saturday. For CSR and in-kind demand in particular, search is where the intent lives and social barely features.

faqs.q: Should our donation page lead with the 80G tax benefit?
faqs.a: No. Since the new tax regime became the default, many individual donors can't claim the deduction at all. Publish your 80G status prominently as a legitimacy signal and explain the receipt process, but lead the page with what the money buys and who it reaches.

faqs.q: How do we get found by corporate CSR teams?
faqs.a: Build a page written for a compliance officer: CSR-1 number, 12A and 80G, audited accounts, the districts you actually operate in, programmes priced as fundable units, an evaluation method, and a named person to email. Then title and structure it around how CSR partners are searched for — cause plus state.

faqs.q: Is Google Ad Grants enough on its own?
faqs.a: It's excellent and it's fragile. The 5% click-through requirement, the keyword restrictions and the $2 cost-per-click cap mean it needs constant attention and can be suspended. It buys head terms while organic compounds; treating it as your only channel means one policy breach removes your entire acquisition.

faqs.q: Should our annual report be a PDF or a web page?
faqs.a: Both, in that order of priority. Publish programme results, financial summaries and impact numbers as web pages that can be linked, updated and cited, then offer the designed PDF as a download. A report that exists only as a PDF earns almost none of the search value it deserves.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take for an NGO?
faqs.a: Local volunteer and in-kind queries can move in eight to twelve weeks, since almost nobody competes properly for them. Cause and donation terms take six to twelve months against large fundraising platforms. CSR partner queries sit in between and convert far better than their volume suggests.
